author: polymorph
text:
That's a good start, fxlife! I've marked up the pic you uploaded a bit more - please don't take this as I'm right and you're wrong. To some degree there is freedom and personal methodology in trading and even in some of the homework. The yellow boxes I drew are other ways you could have marked the blue box that they overlap. That's what the green line vs. the black line in the article is talking about. The outer edge we can agree but the inner edge is some of that freedom I was talking about. Maybe you like to be more selective in your zones and want to see retraces to the wick or maybe you want mark a wider area to watch PA. Either way, the LTF's can help clarify things.

The orange boxes are other areas of supply and demand that I noticed. Take a close look at the box you marked "I drew this zone backwards from here" - what is different about it vs. most of the other zones you drew, like the leftmost one at the top? If you're not sure, head back to the supply and demand article until you see it. But keep posting your charts and enjoy the journey.

author: By_Tor2114
text:
Ok... I'll throw something on the pile!

Although today was a profitable day, I'm going to pin up a trade that I stayed out of. I avoided this one was it was coming up to major USD news. If this had been a HTF entry, the zone would have been wide enough to cope, but it was only about 5 pips wide. I wasn't about to risk losing pips for the sake of volatility! Anyway, on to the setup.

So the M5 chart shows the break of a resistance area. It had made a few FTR steps on the way up, so I was waiting for a something to break in the opposite direction.

If we zoom down to the M1, we get this little flag limit, as highlighted in the ellipse on both charts. You can see a clear engulf of that flag limit, as highlighted by the upwards arrow on the M1 chart. All that was left to do was wait for it to come back up to the sell zone. Don't get me wrong, it's hardly the tidiest setup, but it's something to get the thread rolling again.

author: By_Tor2114
text:
May as well have one more before dealing with a night of curry....

I think the image says it all. A host of FTRs on M1, followed by an engulf in the opposite direction. The sell zone was fairly clear, and it went almost to the pip, but not quite. This is why my orders are always just outside the marked zone.

author: By_Tor2114
text:
And a little bit more for today. I didn't take this trade, as I was too busy monitoring a short on EJ and a long on AUDCHF (Both winners). However, it was such a nice setup that I thought people should get to see it

So, the first look is on M15. We can clearly see a nice break over the top of a resistance area, as marked by the white line.

Zoom into the M1 and we can see where it broke that resistance. It then formed an FTR which was subsequently engulfed to the low side. The sell zone was primed and waiting.

author: By_Tor2114

A sell I just took, but closed waaaaaay too soon! It's the same old setup as the others I've posted, but it's good to see it over and over.

H1 shows the break of a resistance area, as per the white line.

M5 shows the FTR area, and the subsequent break of that FTR.

M1 shows us the obvious sell zone. I initially thought it was going to leave me behind when it made that first move away, but it came back to fill me.

author: danandsueco
text: Let me know where you took the trade and where you closed.

author: By_Tor2114
text:
Opened at the green line. When it made it's way down to where I've put the up arrow, I got spooked by the retrace. I waited for it to go back down, then freaked and closed the trade at that level.

My original plan was to short to the yellow line on this chart. I've been getting better with holding trades, but today was a bit of a relapse.

author: danandsueco
text:
I see this happen all the time. It's actually expected. When I trade, I'll trade the pair until it's done. Few people can predict bottoms and tops. Based on where you closed, how would you be able to short it again? Closing it means, you think it's going to turn.

It's much easier getting out of a trade, good or bad, than sticking to your original plan. In this case, you didn't give your trade a chance. If you planned to close at the blue line, your trade would have still been gaining pips.

author: By_Tor2114
text: I agree. It was certainly a rookie error and one that I'm making less and less. I should have stuck with the original plan of waiting for it to hit the yellow line.

author: By_Tor2114
text:
I should make myself a bit clearer. Just to clarify, I didn't close at the first time it got to that area. When it got there, then retraced, that was what spooked me, so I closed at the second point of returning to that highlighted area.

Still a crappy exit, but it goes to show how emotion can kill a perfectly good trade.

author: danandsueco
text: That's a little worse. Like you said, you closed on emotion when it retraced which makes it worse. The area I marked, is actually a level that could technically be closed at. But then you would sort of be out of a trade and done. If you look at the bigger picture, where I drew the rectangle (not the zone), that PA was very clear leading to a drop off.

author: By_Tor2114
text:
I agree. I'd sat through the worst of the retrace when it came back towards my entry, then exited when it fell back down to the marked zone. It was stupid to hold through the worst of it, then close when it went back in my favour!

Thankfully, I'm doing this less and less. At least I'm picking good entries, which is a good start.
